subject: math
cluster: Work with radicals and integer exponents
intro: Evaluate each square root or cube root, or solve each simple equation. Every number here is a small perfect square or perfect cube. Remember: $x^2 = p$ has two solutions, $x = \pm\sqrt{p}$, while $x^3 = p$ has one real solution, $x = \sqrt[3]{p}$.

steps: The square root of $49$ is the positive number whose square is $49$.
Since $7 \times 7 = 49$, we have $\sqrt{49} = 7$.
Find the positive number whose square is $81$.
Since $9 \times 9 = 81$, we have $\sqrt{81} = 9$.
Find the positive number whose square is $144$.
Since $12 \times 12 = 144$, we have $\sqrt{144} = 12$.
Find the positive number whose square is $25$.
Since $5 \times 5 = 25$, we have $\sqrt{25} = 5$.
Find the positive number whose square is $100$.
Since $10 \times 10 = 100$, we have $\sqrt{100} = 10$.
The cube root of $27$ is the number whose cube is $27$.
Since $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$, we have $\sqrt[3]{27} = 3$.
Find the number whose cube is $8$.
Since $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$, we have $\sqrt[3]{8} = 2$.
Find the number whose cube is $64$.
Since $4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64$, we have $\sqrt[3]{64} = 4$.
Note: $\sqrt[3]{64} = 4$, not $8$. The square root of $64$ is $8$, but the cube root is $4$.
Find the number whose cube is $125$.
Since $5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125$, we have $\sqrt[3]{125} = 5$.
Find the number whose cube is $1$.
Since $1 \times 1 \times 1 = 1$, we have $\sqrt[3]{1} = 1$.
Take the square root of both sides. An equation of the form $x^2 = p$ has two solutions.
$x = \pm\sqrt{36}$
Since $6 \times 6 = 36$, we get $x = \pm 6$.
Take the square root of both sides: $x = \pm\sqrt{121}$.
Since $11 \times 11 = 121$, we get $x = \pm 11$.
Remember to include both the positive and negative root.
Take the square root of both sides: $x = \pm\sqrt{9}$.
Since $3 \times 3 = 9$, we get $x = \pm 3$.
Take the cube root of both sides. An equation of the form $x^3 = p$ has one real solution.
Since $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$, we get $x = 2$.
There is no $\pm$ for a cube root; $(-2)^3 = -8$, not $8$.
Take the cube root of both sides: $x = \sqrt[3]{27}$.
Since $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$, we get $x = 3$.
Only the single value $x = 3$ works, because $(-3)^3 = -27$.
